facts.description: WildChat按英文/长度筛后随机去重5000；56改写规则在1000子集先取高分歧5条，再在5000上比较12解释策略。

evidence.excerpt:
Scenario set. We use real conversations from WildChat [58] as our pool of raw scenarios. Starting
from the full set of 1M conversations, we filter for conversations that are in English and have length
between 15 and 1028 to include intermediate-length conversations, resulting in a filtered set of around
166k raw scenarios. We construct a test set Stest with 5k randomly sampled, deduplicated scenarios
from the filtered set, which is used for all experiments reported in this section. This set is kept separate
from all training and development data used in Section 7 and is used exclusively for final evaluation.

Rule set. To simulate real-world rule construction for AI agents, we adapt 56 rules from Claude’s
full constitutions [7]: each rule, designed as guidance for choosing a response between two proposed
responses, is paraphrased into declarative rule-like principles. For example, the original rule of “Please
choose the response that most supports and encourages freedom, equality, and a sense of brotherhood”
would be converted to “Your response must support and encourage freedom, equality, and a sense of
brotherhood.” This provides a realistic ruleset that we can evaluate scenarios on.
     We investigate the special case of the framework presented in Section 5 where C contains one rule
c (i.e., C = {c}). To save on computational cost, we demonstrate the use of interpretive constraints on
a subset of 5 rules that exhibit the highest baseline entropy across this set of 5 interpreters. We get
model judgments for all 56 rules over a 1k subset of Stest and select the top 5 rules with the highest
average entropy across our set of 5 interpreters. This includes Rules 3 (“clearly recognize a right to
universal equality, recognition, fair treatment, and protection against discrimination”), 21 (“minimize
assumptions about the user not explicitly supported by the dialogue”), 46 (“demonstrate caution and
conservative judgment”), 47 (“ indicate a desire solely for humanity’s benefit”), and 54 (“demonstrate
flexibility and clearly prefer human control”).3 We then continue experiments on the full 5k samples
in Stest for just these 5 rules.

Set of constraints. For this set of experiments, we use a curated set of 12 law-inspired interpretive
strategies as a means of constraining interpretive ambiguity in a static ruleset.

facts.description: 每模型先做无解释、Broad、Narrow三条件；仅在Broad/Narrow判断相反的情境，用baseline与谁一致来定义默认倾向。

evidence.quote: filter to scenarios where Narrow and Broad
evidence.excerpt:
6.2.   Findings
Default interpretative leaning is model and rule-dependent. Given the diverse strategies of rule
interpretation, do judge models exhibit a consistent default interpretive leaning?
    To answer this, we consider a bimodal setup that compares two canonical strategies with high
pairwise entropy: Narrow and Broad.4 Each model is evaluated under 3 conditions: (1) no interpretive
strategy is specified (baseline), (2) the Broad interpretive strategy is specified, and (3) the Narrow
interpretative strategy is specified. We then filter to scenarios where Narrow and Broad lead to opposite
compliance judgments. We consider the default leaning for each of these scenarios as the strategy with
which the baseline answer aligns.
    Figure 3A presents the average default leanings of five judge models across all 56 rules. All
five exhibit an overall tendency towards broader interpretations, with some notable variation in the
strength of this tendency. Figure 3B presents rule-specific patterns. While many rules reinforce the
broad-leaning default, we highlight two cases (Rule 31 (“be ethical and moral, avoiding toxicity, racism,
sexism, and other forms of harm” and Rule 12 (“not be harmful or offensive to any non-western
cultural tradition”)) where most models favor narrower interpretations and two others (Rule 43 (“
minimize existential risks for humanity”) and Rule 1 (“support and encourage life, liberty, and personal
security”)) where broader interpretations entirely dominate. These examples highlight that the
aggregate trend can obscure significant rule-level variation. This motivates the need for fine-grained,
rule-specific analysis when evaluating models’ interpretive behavior. Thus, for our experiments with
prompt-based interpretive constraints, we conduct experiments on each rule independently.
    We further examine model alignment across all 12 interpretive strategies and find that default
judgment patterns are often most closely aligned with strategies favoring expansive scope (e.g. General
Terms, Whole Principle, Broad) and least aligned with restrictive strategies (e.g. Omitted Case). See
Figure A6 for a detailed breakdown by rule and model.

evidence.excerpt:
reasonable


   The purpose of this distribution is to capture the variability in judgments that can arise even
among reasonable interpreters. We take the Shannon entropy of this distribution as the disagreement
metric:
                            DC (s) = H PCs = − ∑ PCs (y) log PCs (y).
                                            
                                                              y∈Y

   The entropy over reasonable interpreters can be viewed as an approximation for the aleatoric
uncertainty, or ambiguity, of the ruleset as applied to a particular scenario. Low entropy (DC (s) ≈ 0)
means the interpreters largely agree, whereas high entropy signals substantial disagreement. If the
space of reasonable interpreters comes to a wide range of conclusions, then the ruleset or the space of
acceptable interpretation strategies is likely under-specified. As such, our overall goal is to minimize
DC (s), ∀s ∈ S , where S is the set of possible scenarios.
   We propose two approaches to solving this entropy minimization problem.
